title: Ancient Petra
summary: How the Nabataeans carved the city of Petra into rose-colored sandstone cliffs, grew rich from caravan trade, and stored water in the desert.
poll: Ancient cities like Petra are worth protecting, even though no one lives in them today.

versions.title: The Rock City
versions.text:
There is an old city in the desert. It is in Jordan. Its name is Petra. It is made of rock!

Long ago, a group of Arabs lived there. They were the Nabataeans. They did not use bricks. They cut homes in the cliff. They cut tombs, too. To cut rock like this is to carve it. They worked hard. It was a big job.

The rock is pink and red. So it has a nick name too. It is the Rose City.

You walk in on a long path. It is thin. Rock walls rise up on each side. Look up! They are so tall. Then you see a huge tomb. It is called the Treasury.

They were good at trade. Camels came to the city. They brought spice to sell. They brought things that smell sweet. The town got rich.

It is hot and dry there. It does not rain much in the desert. So the folks made dams. They made pipes. They kept the rain to use.

They carved tombs in Saudi Arabia, too. You can see them at Hegra. It is near AlUla.

Now, lots of folks come to see Petra each year.

To get in, you walk down a long, thin path. Tall rock walls rise on both sides. At the end, you see a huge carved front. It is called the Treasury. But it was really a tomb.

The Nabataeans were great at trade. Lines of camels came through the city. They brought spice to sell. They brought things that smell sweet. The city grew rich.

It does not rain much in the desert. So they built dams and pipes. They saved the rain to use later.

They also carved tombs in Saudi Arabia. You can see them at Hegra, near AlUla.

Now lots of people visit Petra each year. Would you like to go?

versions.title: Ancient Petra
versions.text:
Deep in the desert of Jordan is a city made of stone. Its name is Petra. Its buildings were not made with bricks. They were cut right into the rock!

More than two thousand years ago, a group of Arabs lived here. They were called the Nabataeans. Petra was their main city. They were good at their work. They carved homes and tombs into the cliff walls. To carve means to cut a shape out of something hard.

The rock here is pink, red, and orange. That is why people call it the Rose City.

To reach Petra, you walk down a narrow path. Very tall rock walls stand on each side. At the end of the path, a huge carved building appears. It is called the Treasury. But it was really a tomb, maybe for a king.

The Nabataeans grew rich from trade. Long lines of camels came through Petra. They carried spices to sell. They brought incense that smells sweet. The traders paid to stop and rest there.

Petra is in a dry desert. So water was very important. The Nabataeans built dams and pipes. They made deep tanks to catch and save rain.

The Nabataeans also carved tombs in Saudi Arabia. They are at Hegra, near AlUla. Today, many visitors come to see both places.

Those people were the Nabataeans, an Arab people who established Petra as their capital. They were talented builders who carved homes, tombs, and enormous halls into the cliffs, working from the top downward so that falling rock would not damage completed sections. Their engineering skill is still admired by modern architects.

The cliffs consist of sandstone, a relatively soft rock that appears in bands of pink, red, and orange. Because of these warm colors, Petra is frequently called the Rose City.

To enter the city, visitors travel through the Siq, a narrow, winding canyon with towering rock walls. At the end of the canyon, an enormous carved facade suddenly appears. It is called the Treasury, because of an old legend about hidden gold, but it was actually a tomb, probably created for a Nabataean king.

The Nabataeans became wealthy through trade. Long camel caravans transported spices and fragrant incense from southern Arabia through Petra, and the traders paid the Nabataeans to rest there and collect water before continuing their journey north.

Because Petra is located in a dry desert, water was extremely valuable. The Nabataeans constructed dams, clay pipes, and deep underground tanks called cisterns to capture and store rainwater, which allowed thousands of people to live there comfortably.

Over time, traders began shipping goods by sea instead, and the city slowly declined. After a powerful earthquake damaged many buildings, Petra was gradually abandoned, although local Bedouin families continued to live nearby.

The Nabataeans also carved tombs in Saudi Arabia, at Hegra near AlUla, which became the Kingdom's first World Heritage Site. Today, visitors from around the world travel to explore both remarkable places.

versions.title: Ancient Petra
versions.text:
Deep within the desert expanses of southern Jordan lies an ancient city that was carved directly from solid stone rather than assembled, brick by brick, in the usual manner. Its name is Petra, and its most celebrated monuments were carved directly into the surrounding mountainsides by a people who inhabited the region more than two thousand years ago, during an era when the city ranked among the wealthiest settlements anywhere in Arabia.

Those people were the Nabataeans, an Arab civilization that established Petra as its capital. They proved themselves exceptionally skilled builders, carving elaborate homes, tombs, and enormous ceremonial halls directly into the surrounding cliffs, working from the top of each formation downward so that falling rock would not damage sections already completed below. Their engineering accomplishments continue to impress modern architects and archaeologists alike.

The surrounding cliffs consist mainly of sandstone, a fairly soft rock that naturally appears in distinctive bands of pink, red, and orange. Because of these warm colors, Petra is often described as the Rose City, a nickname made popular by nineteenth-century European travelers.

To enter the city, visitors must pass through the Siq, a narrow, winding canyon enclosed on both sides by towering rock walls. At the end of this dramatic canyon, an enormous carved facade unexpectedly appears before the visitor. It is popularly known as the Treasury, because of an old local legend about hidden gold. In historical reality, though, it functioned as a monumental tomb, almost certainly made for a Nabataean king.

The Nabataeans grew prosperous through steady trade, since long camel caravans carried fragrant spices and precious incense from southern Arabia through Petra on their way elsewhere, and the traveling merchants paid the Nabataeans for the chance to rest there and refill their water before continuing their journey northward.

Because Petra sits in a thoroughly dry desert location, water was an extraordinarily valuable resource, so the resourceful Nabataeans built dams, clay pipes, and deep underground storage tanks called cisterns specifically to capture and keep seasonal rainwater, an achievement that let thousands of people live there in real comfort and even grow gardens.

Eventually, however, merchants increasingly began shipping their goods by sea instead of overland, and the city consequently declined in importance; after a powerful earthquake damaged many buildings, Petra was gradually abandoned by most of its original residents, although local Bedouin families still lived in the surrounding area for generations afterward.

The Nabataeans also carved similar tombs within present-day Saudi Arabia, at Hegra near AlUla, which later became the Kingdom's very first officially designated World Heritage Site. Today, visitors from around the world travel considerable distances to explore both of these remarkable sites and to learn more about the civilization that created them. Remarkably, the Nabataeans also developed their own alphabet, which gradually evolved, over many centuries, into the Arabic script still used today.

versions.title: Ancient Petra
versions.text:
Deep within the arid desert expanses of southern Jordan lies an ancient city that was meticulously carved directly from solid stone rather than laboriously assembled, brick by brick, in the conventional architectural manner. Its name is Petra, and its most celebrated monuments were sculpted directly into the surrounding mountainsides by a sophisticated people who inhabited the region more than two thousand years ago, during an era when the city ranked prominently among the wealthiest settlements anywhere in the Arabian Peninsula.

Those remarkable people were the Nabataeans, an Arab civilization that established Petra as its political, religious, and commercial capital. They proved themselves exceptionally skilled and inventive builders, carving elaborate residences, tombs, and enormous ceremonial halls directly into the surrounding cliff faces, methodically working from the summit of each rock formation downward precisely so that falling debris would not damage sections of the carving already completed below. Their considerable engineering accomplishments continue to impress contemporary architects and archaeologists alike, more than two full millennia after their creation.

The surrounding cliffs themselves consist predominantly of sandstone, a comparatively soft sedimentary rock that naturally appears in distinctive, striated bands of pink, red, and orange hues formed over geological time. Owing to these warm, striking colors, Petra is frequently and affectionately described by visitors as the Rose City, a nickname that was itself popularized by nineteenth-century European travelers who first documented and publicized the site to a wider audience.

To enter the ancient city proper, visitors must traverse the Siq, a narrow, winding natural canyon enclosed on both sides by towering, shadow-casting rock walls. At the culminating end of this dramatic canyon, an enormous carved facade unexpectedly appears before the awestruck visitor; it is popularly known as the Treasury, owing to a persistent old local legend concerning concealed gold supposedly hidden within, though in documented historical reality it functioned as a monumental royal tomb, almost certainly created for a Nabataean king of considerable stature.

The Nabataeans grew substantially prosperous through sustained, carefully managed trade, since long camel caravans transported fragrant spices and precious incense from southern Arabia through Petra en route to markets elsewhere, and the traveling merchants duly compensated the Nabataeans for the valuable opportunity to rest there safely and replenish their essential water supplies before continuing their arduous journey northward toward distant markets.

Because Petra occupies a thoroughly arid desert location with minimal natural rainfall, water constituted an extraordinarily valuable and carefully managed resource, so the remarkably resourceful Nabataeans constructed dams, clay pipes, and deep underground storage tanks called cisterns specifically to capture and preserve seasonal rainwater, an impressive engineering achievement that collectively allowed thousands of residents to live there in genuine comfort and even to cultivate flourishing ornamental gardens within an otherwise hostile environment.

Eventually, however, merchants increasingly began transporting their goods by sea rather than overland, and the city consequently declined considerably in sustained commercial importance over subsequent generations; after a powerful earthquake subsequently damaged numerous buildings throughout the settlement, Petra was progressively abandoned by the majority of its original inhabitants, although local Bedouin families nevertheless continued to inhabit the surrounding region for many generations thereafter, maintaining a continuous human presence.

The Nabataeans also carved comparable monumental tombs within present-day Saudi Arabia, specifically at Hegra near AlUla, a site that subsequently became the Kingdom's very first officially designated World Heritage Site. Today, visitors from around the entire world travel considerable distances to explore both of these remarkable archaeological locations and to investigate more thoroughly the sophisticated civilization that originally created them. Remarkably, the Nabataeans also developed their own distinctive written alphabet, one that gradually evolved, over many subsequent centuries of linguistic change, into the Arabic script still used throughout the world today.

MID.modelAnswer: The Nabataeans solved the problem of living in a dry desert by building dams, clay pipes, and deep tanks to capture and store rainwater. They also solved the problem of needing shelter by carving their homes and tombs directly into the sandstone cliffs instead of building with bricks. These clever solutions let the Nabataeans live and trade successfully in a difficult desert environment.

HIGH.prompt: Which achievement of the Nabataeans do you think was most impressive: their carving, their trade, or their water system? Support your claim with evidence from the article.
checklist: I made a clear claim about one achievement.
I supported my claim with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained my reasoning and used correct grammar and punctuation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe the Nabataeans' water system was their most impressive achievement. Petra lies in a dry desert, yet the Nabataeans built dams, clay pipes, and deep cisterns to capture and store rainwater, allowing an entire city to thrive where water should have been scarce. This system also supported their trade, since camel caravans carrying spices and incense could stop in Petra to rest and collect water. Without solving the water problem first, the Nabataeans' famous carvings and caravan trade through the city would never have been possible.
